compiler_and_flags: Mesh built with gcc 8 -O3 -flto; SPEC with clang 4.0 -O2
hardware: MacBook Pro, Intel i7-5600U, 16 GiB RAM, Linux 4.18 Ubuntu Bionic
name: Mesh
baseline: jemalloc (Firefox, Redis); glibc malloc (SPEC CPU2006, Ruby)
workload: Heap size of Firefox 57 (Speedometer), Redis 4.0.2 with fragmenting workload and SPECint2006 under Mesh compaction versus default allocator, with runtime overhead measured.
claimed_speedup: Not a speed win: reduces Firefox heap 16% and Redis 39% versus jemalloc (paper); runtime overhead is low (Redis insertion within 2% of jemalloc).
tradeoffs: Compacting via page meshing needs virtual-memory remapping; Linux and macOS only, Windows work in progress; Bazel build; some workloads gain nothing.
caveats: Peer-reviewed PLDI 2019 paper but benchmark scripts and flags for baselines not fully public; old baselines (jemalloc 3.6.0, glibc 2.26); the claim is memory footprint, not throughput.
found_via: mimalloc-bench README allocator list (daanx/mimalloc-bench), then plasma-umass/mesh repo and checked-in PLDI paper

name: IsoAlloc
workload: Repeated alloc/free, calloc/free and realloc/free loop (1834784 tests) via the repo's own test binary, compared with glibc and jemalloc LD_PRELOAD.
claimed_speedup: iso_alloc/free 0.081s versus malloc/free about 0.66-0.72s; calloc 1.04s versus about 2.71s; realloc 0.83s versus about 1.84-1.94s (derived from page data; pairing of rows to glibc is read from PERFORMANCE.md layout); roughly on par with jemalloc (0.0846s alloc/free).
tradeoffs: Security-focused (guard pages, canaries, bitmap zones, double-free detection); higher memory use; 64-bit Linux and macOS only.
caveats: First-party microbenchmark, compiler flags not stated; project itself calls the allocator 'fast(ish)'; glibc rows identified by position in the file, verify before relying.
found_via: mimalloc-bench README allocator list, then struct/isoalloc PERFORMANCE.md

name: micromalloc
workload: Same-thread and cross-thread alloc/dealloc plus Larson, measuring Mops/s and memory overhead ratio against glibc 2.17, jemalloc 5.3.0, mimalloc 1.8 and snmalloc 3.14.
claimed_speedup: Memory overhead very close to glibc but with better performance; cross-thread: slower than snmalloc and jemalloc yet above glibc with the lowest memory overhead; Larson scales well. No exact numbers (plots only).
tradeoffs: Low memory overhead by design; usually slower than mimalloc, snmalloc, tbbmalloc, jemalloc; O(1) alloc and free; can allocate from preallocated buffers or memory-mapped files.
caveats: README admits it is usually not faster than mimalloc, jemalloc or snmalloc; the claim to beat glibc is shown only as plots; first-party; flags not stated.
found_via: WebSearch: memory allocator benchmark shootout drop-in malloc faster than mimalloc jemalloc

compiler_and_flags: Release -O3 -march=native with LTO (build configuration; not confirmed as the benchmark build)
hardware: 2-vCPU VM (CPU model not stated); glibc 2.41, jemalloc 5.3.0, mimalloc 2.1.7
name: FastAlloc
workload: Cross-allocator matrix of churn and related workloads at several thread counts plus memory retention after freeing 1M objects and p50/p99 latency, on a 2-vCPU VM.
claimed_speedup: Wins 20/33 throughput cells versus glibc, 21/33 versus jemalloc, 12/33 versus mimalloc; small blocks 1.24-2.98x faster; retains 16.0 MB versus 46.7/171.8/552.2 MB (glibc/jemalloc/mimalloc) after freeing 1M objects.
tradeoffs: TLS caches with lock-free MPSC queues, adaptive slabs, returns empty slabs to OS; optional memory-safety instrumentation mode; Windows and Linux.
caveats: Self-reported; loses a majority of cells against mimalloc (12/33 wins); tiny 2-vCPU VM; CPU model missing; latest commit is a 'restore repository to baseline' reset so history may be unstable; very new.
found_via: WebSearch: new memory allocator C++ github faster than mimalloc

name: Bloodmoon001 pool memory allocator
workload: Fixed-size pool allocator microbenchmarks: single int alloc+dealloc, std::string create+destroy, 10,000 bulk allocations and throughput.
claimed_speedup: Single int 2,731 ns versus 29,067 ns (10.6x); std::string 7,240 ns versus 19,826 ns (2.7x); bulk 10,000 allocations 54,860 ns versus 433,902 ns (7.9x); throughput 188 M ops/sec versus 23 M ops/sec (8.1x).
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 pool allocator, O(1) alloc/free, intrusive free list; fixed-size blocks, not a general malloc replacement.
caveats: Comparison is a pool allocator versus general-purpose malloc (not like for like); Windows CRT malloc baseline; no mimalloc/jemalloc comparison; 3 commits, brand new; page numbers are from README.
found_via: WebSearch: new memory allocator C++ github faster than mimalloc

name: Exgen-Malloc
workload: Single-threaded allocator designed for single-threaded programs, evaluated on SPEC CPU2017 and mimalloc-bench.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean 1.19x over dlmalloc and 1.03x over mimalloc on SPEC CPU2017; 6.2% memory savings versus mimalloc on SPEC CPU2017, up to 25.2% on mimalloc-bench.
tradeoffs: Not thread-safe by design: omits remote-free and concurrency control; suited to single-threaded programs.
caveats: Snippet only: arxiv.org and the CAL PDF not opened (egress blocked); numbers from search-result summary; no repository found, so has_code=false; flags and CPU unverified.
found_via: WebSearch: malloc benchmark comparison mimalloc jemalloc tcmalloc snmalloc results
